entries.name: Breadth-first branch-and-bound search
entries.definition: A heuristic graph-search procedure that expands states in breadth-first layers and prunes candidate paths whose accumulated cost plus an admissible remaining-cost estimate exceeds a supplied solution-cost bound; the formulation curated here assumes uniform positive edge costs, scaled to one.
entries.identity_notes: The BFBnB search strategy is distinguished from BFIDA*, which obtains bounds by repeated searches, and from width-pruned beam search. Breadth-first heuristic search names the broader family in Zhou and Hansen; that umbrella phrase is not asserted as an exact alias. Frontier, sparse-memory and layered duplicate-detection implementations are alternatives, not mandatory simultaneous components.
entries.mechanism: For a unit-cost graph, process nodes by increasing depth g and evaluate f=g+h with admissible h. Under a hypothetical bound U, retain f≤U. If U is the cost of an actual retained incumbent and only improvement is needed, f≥U can instead be pruned; failure to improve then preserves the incumbent. Memory-saving implementations retain enough information for duplicate detection and use relay nodes to reconstruct a found path by recursively solving subproblems.
entries.locator: Sections 3–3.5, printed pp. 389–395 / PDF pp. 5–11; Figure 2 and the actual-incumbent versus hypothetical-bound distinction on printed pp. 393–394
limitations: The scope is uniform positive costs and an admissible heuristic. A valid upper bound must cover a real solution for a single-pass optimal-solution guarantee; an unsuccessful hypothetical contour does not establish that the original problem is unsolvable.
The layered implementation needs enough previous-layer information for the graph structure; retaining one previous layer is not a universal duplicate-elimination rule for directed graphs.
Memory-saving implementations can still run out of memory in a large frontier. The paper explicitly does not prove universally lower peak memory than best-first search.

The f≥U option is valid for improving an actual incumbent, not for an inclusive hypothetical contour with no stored solution. Preserving the incumbent when no improvement exists is an explicit operational consequence of that distinction.
The record does not certify the printed pseudocode for all base cases, graph-locality claims under every pruning policy, or nonuniform-cost extensions.

additional_evidence.claim: The authors consider frontier, sparse-memory and layered duplicate handling, and relay-based path recovery. The potential reduction in stored search nodes is problem dependent; neither a fixed total-memory bound nor a universal advantage over A* follows. Nonuniform-cost extensions are outlined as future work.
additional_evidence.locator: Sections 2.2–3.4, 6.1–6.2; printed pp. 387–392 and 405–406 / PDF pp. 3–8 and 21–22

entries.name: Breadth-first iterative-deepening A-star
entries.definition: An iterative-deepening heuristic graph-search algorithm that repeatedly runs breadth-first branch-and-bound within increasing hypothetical f=g+h cost bounds, beginning at the start-state f value, until a solution is found; the curated formulation uses unit edge costs and a nonnegative admissible heuristic with h(goal)=0.
entries.identity_notes: BFIDA* changes the inner traversal of cost-contour iterative deepening to breadth-first branch-and-bound. It is distinct from depth-first IDA*, depth-limited iterative-deepening DFS, and a single BFBnB search with a supplied incumbent bound. The memory implementation can use frontier or layered duplicate handling.
entries.mechanism: Set T=f(start). Run breadth-first branch-and-bound admitting nodes with f≤T. If no goal is reached, restart with a larger T, such as the least f value excluded on the preceding pass; the paper also describes increments of one in its unit-cost setting. Repeat until a solution is found. Breadth-first traversal, admissible pruning and sufficient resources preserve a minimum-cost solution in this uniform-cost setting.
entries.locator: Section 4, printed p. 395 / PDF p. 11; Section 3.5 Figure 2, printed p. 394 / PDF p. 10
limitations: The hypothetical threshold is inclusive. Reusing strict incumbent pruning at T=f(start) without a retained solution would be a different procedure.
This method repeats breadth-first contours and retains frontier/duplicate information; it does not inherit the path-linear storage of depth-first IDA*.

The asymptotic node-expansion analysis assumes exponential growth of distinct nodes per iteration; the directed-graph result additionally constrains solution depth relative to stored layers. It is not an unconditional wall-clock optimum.
Large layers and tie contours can still be costly. Solvable finite-depth cases require sufficient memory; no universal termination guarantee on infinite unsolvable graphs is asserted.

additional_evidence.claim: The expansion-count theorems depend on growth assumptions, while breadth-first traversal restricts beneficial tie-breaking within a contour. Memory remains governed by the retained search frontier and duplicate-detection strategy.
additional_evidence.locator: Section 4.1 Theorems 4–5, Section 4.2, and Section 6.2; printed pp. 396–397 and 406 / PDF pp. 12–13 and 22

entries.name: Divide-and-conquer beam search
entries.definition: A memory-limited breadth-first heuristic search that discards least-promising open nodes when its chosen capacity is reached and recovers a solution through relay-based divide-and-conquer reconstruction instead of retaining every predecessor layer.
entries.identity_notes: Divide-and-conquer beam search is the approximate search procedure introduced by Zhou and Hansen in 2004. It differs from divide-and-conquer beam-stack search, which adds systematic backtracking and replay under saved beam ranges. Relay reconstruction alone does not revisit every branch discarded by beam pruning.
entries.mechanism: Use breadth-first heuristic search with layered duplicate handling and relay pointers. When memory is full, remove open nodes with the worst evaluation values and continue with the surviving beam. On reaching a goal, recover its path by recursively searching the start-to-relay and relay-to-goal subproblems. Those reconstruction searches can find shorter subpaths, but this does not restore a global completeness or optimality guarantee.
entries.locator: Divide-and-Conquer Beam Search, PDF p. 6; Figure 3 and path reconstruction, PDF p. 5; experimental implementation description, PDF p. 8
limitations: Permanent width pruning can discard every solution path; ordinary DCBS is neither complete nor guaranteed optimal.
The reported current, previous, next and relay layers count retained search-node layers, not all temporary successors, recursive reconstruction state or output storage.

The original developed search setting has uniform edge costs. Its planning implementation uses an inadmissible additive heuristic for ranking and a separate admissible heuristic for lower bounds; ranking and safe cost pruning must not be conflated.
Larger permitted beams and reconstruction improvements do not establish monotonic quality or a universal speed advantage.

entries.name: Best-first beam search with per-length budgets
entries.definition: The sequence-decoding beam procedure of Meister, Vieira and Cotterell that prioritizes active hypotheses by decreasing accumulated score, breaks score ties by shorter length, and limits accepted expansions to k hypotheses at each sequence length without a future-score heuristic.
entries.identity_notes: This is the 2020 sequence-decoding meaning of best-first beam search. Its per-length budget is distinct from AIMech:GlobalFrontierBeamSearch, which caps the entire open list. The qualified name avoids treating those different pruning rules as exact synonyms. The h=0 procedure is a specialization of the paper’s A-star beam framework.
entries.mechanism: Maintain a score-prioritized agenda and a count for each hypothesis length; skip expansion after k hypotheses of that length have been accepted. Under scores that never increase on extension and h=0, the paper shows that the top completed hypothesis agrees with its specified width-k layer beam, with compatible tie and EOS conventions. Once k hypotheses of a later length have been accepted, earlier unfinished layers can be removed under those same monotonicity assumptions.
entries.locator: Algorithm 2 and Table 1, printed pp. 797–798 / PDF pp. 3–4; Sections 3.2–4.1, printed pp. 798–801 / PDF pp. 4–7
limitations: The finite beam is an approximation to exact sequence-model decoding; equality to a specified beam procedure is not global MAP optimality.

Sequence length limits, EOS handling and compatible deterministic tie conventions are part of the comparison. Arbitrary implementations with different stopping or tie rules need not return identical hypotheses.

Queue counts are counts of retained hypotheses, not total bytes including neural states, model parameters, backpointers and temporary successors. No numerical speedup or benchmark-quality claim is curated.

The beam-equivalence claim is restricted to nonincreasing scores and h=0. The paper also asserts a nonmonotonic stop-only extension; this record does not adopt that guarantee because a saved curator finite-tree counterexample exposes a conflict with unchanged per-length pruning.
The optimized queue-of-beams representation can retain hypotheses at several lengths. The per-length budget is not a global queue-capacity bound.

entries.name: A-star beam search for sequence decoding
aliases: A* beam search for sequence decoding
entries.definition: A sequence-decoding beam framework that ranks active hypotheses by accumulated score plus an optimistic future-score heuristic, uses shorter length to break score ties, and limits accepted expansions to k hypotheses per sequence length.
entries.identity_notes: This names the finite-beam A-star decoding framework in Meister, Vieira and Cotterell, not every algorithm informally called A-star beam search. The h=0 specialization has its own per-length best-first record. A finite per-length budget distinguishes the framework from unpruned A* and from a whole-frontier capacity cap.
entries.mechanism: Use Algorithm 2 with the A-star beam settings in Table 1: prioritize the sum of current score and h, maintain a separate length counter, and suppress expansions beyond that length’s k budget. For maximization, an admissible h is optimistic about achievable future reward. The framework’s top-completed-hypothesis stopping rule operates over this already-pruned agenda; a finite beam can exclude globally superior paths.
entries.locator: Section 3, Algorithm 2 and Table 1; Definition 3.1; printed pp. 797–798 / PDF pp. 3–4
limitations: The finite beam is an approximation to exact sequence-model decoding; equality to a specified beam procedure is not global MAP optimality.

Sequence length limits, EOS handling and compatible deterministic tie conventions are part of the comparison. Arbitrary implementations with different stopping or tie rules need not return identical hypotheses.

Queue counts are counts of retained hypotheses, not total bytes including neural states, model parameters, backpointers and temporary successors. No numerical speedup or benchmark-quality claim is curated.
Admissibility of h does not preserve the zero-heuristic beam’s output after finite pruning. This is explicitly acknowledged in Section 4.1.
Unpruned A-star guarantees cannot be transferred to the finite-beam framework merely because its heuristic is admissible. No unrestricted nonmonotonic stopping theorem is asserted.
Application to a particular score requires checking the direction and validity of its future-reward bound, terminal behavior and stopping policy.

entries.name: Memory-reduced best-first beam search for sequence decoding
entries.definition: A capacity-limited variant of per-length best-first sequence beam search that, when its chosen total queue capacity is reached, removes the worst-scoring active hypothesis from the earliest active sequence length.
entries.identity_notes: This is the memory-reduced variant in Meister, Vieira and Cotterell Section 3.3. Its eviction first chooses the earliest active length, so it differs from globally removing the worst-ranked hypothesis. It also differs from the base per-length best-first procedure, which can retain hypotheses at several lengths without this extra capacity pruning.
entries.mechanism: Organize active hypotheses in queues for their sequence lengths and prioritize lengths by their best available score. Apply the base per-length beam limits and an additional total active-queue capacity. To make room, evict the minimum-scoring item in the earliest nonempty length queue; then continue decoding the surviving agenda.
entries.locator: Section 3.3, Memory-Reduced Best-First Beam Search, printed pp. 799–800 / PDF pp. 5–6
limitations: The finite beam is an approximation to exact sequence-model decoding; equality to a specified beam procedure is not global MAP optimality.

Sequence length limits, EOS handling and compatible deterministic tie conventions are part of the comparison. Arbitrary implementations with different stopping or tie rules need not return identical hypotheses.

Queue counts are counts of retained hypotheses, not total bytes including neural states, model parameters, backpointers and temporary successors. No numerical speedup or benchmark-quality claim is curated.
Additional capacity eviction can remove paths retained by the unmodified beam procedure, so its same-output guarantee is not inherited. The memory/quality tradeoff is empirical and problem dependent.
The queue cap does not bound the entire decoder or neural model memory. The earliest-length eviction is not a global worst-score eviction rule.
No guarantee for arbitrary nonmonotonic scores or globally optimal sequence decoding is asserted.

curator_analysis.claim_tested: Whether changing only termination restores standard-beam equivalence for arbitrary nonmonotone scores with unchanged per-length expansion limits.
curator_analysis.observation: At width 2 the layer beam returns a completion scored 10; the curator’s per-length best-first procedure with an exact remaining-completion upper bound returns -5 after the superior depth-two hypothesis is rejected by its already-used budget. Optional older-layer pruning is absent.
curator_analysis.interpretation: This is evidence against the unrestricted stop-only claim under the stated finite-tree interpretation. It is not a benchmark or execution of the authors’ implementation, and does not challenge the monotone-score method.
limits: This implementation specializes a finite depth-three tree and stores complete hypotheses as incumbents instead of repeated EOS padding.
The optional monotonicity-based older-layer deletion is deliberately not used; the per-length limit alone produces the discrepancy.
All complete paths have the same length, ties do not determine the result, and successor-score increments can represent an additively decomposable nonprobabilistic scoring function.
A primary correction or stronger nonmonotonic algorithm could add conditions or change pruning; that remains a separate evidence check.
